abstract: Single-cell genomics has been instrumental for studying the variation between cell states. Yet, the use of single-cell technologies to study variation between sample groups remains challenging, with findings often failing to replicate across cohorts. Here, we introduce a general framework for robust single-cell analysis that uses subsampling of individuals to identify statistical patterns that hold regardless of which unmeasured characteristics of those individuals covary with the condition of interest. Within this framework, a t-test for differential expression, a chi-squared test for differential composition, and a linear projection for contrastive representation learning outperform state-of-the-art alternatives in cross-cohort replicability. This identifies robustness by design, rather than refined distributional assumptions and model expressiveness, as a principal driver of reproducible discovery in single-cell studies. Applying robust contrastive learning to naive CD4 T cells from human blood, we uncover eleven replicating age-associated subpopulations, largely uncharacterized, that express programs of other states and go undetected by standard analysis. One of them is most strongly defined by CTLA4, a checkpoint receptor considered a hallmark of antigen-experienced and regulatory T cells, yet carries a naive surface phenotype and is distinct from regulatory T cells. This population is conserved in mice and increases in frequency with age in both the CD4 and CD8 compartments. Upon stimulation, these cells exhibit attenuated proliferation compared with conventional naive T cells and enrichment of regulatory phenotypes. Blocking CTLA4 signaling largely restores the downstream activation program to that of conventional naive cells, suggesting these cells may be a reversible contributor to the age-associated decline in naive T-cell responsiveness. By prioritizing robustness over richer models, our framework enables discovery of previously hidden cellular heterogeneity and offers a general strategy for improving resolution and replicability in single-cell genomics. Code is available at github.com/robust-precision-medicine.
